question_details.title: Will the US eliminate the Department of Education through law or presidential reorganization before 2026?
question_details.description:
This question is synced with an identical question on Metaculus. The original question opened on 2024-12-20 21:00:00 and can be found [here](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/31076). This question will resolve to the same value as the synced question. The original question's background info at this time is below. 

President-elect Donald Trump [stated during his presidential campaign](https://www.cnn.com/2023/09/13/politics/trump-department-of-education-states-2024/index.html) that he wants to eliminate the Department of Education. Since winning the presidential election he has stood by this statement. In his 2024 Person of the Year [interview with Time](https://time.com/7201565/person-of-the-year-2024-donald-trump-transcript/) (conducted November 25, 2024 and published December 12, 2024), he responded to questions about his plan to cut government spending as follows:

> **\[Time:] What do you plan to do?**
>  
> \[Trump:] I mean, I'll give you an example. We want to move the schools back to the states. We want to, you know, we're at the bottom of every list in terms of education, and we're at the top of the list in terms of the cost per pupil, and we want to move them back to the states, and we'll spend half the money on a much better product. We'll get—I believe we can compete with Norway and Denmark and Finland and other countries. And I will tell you, China is right at the top of the list too. Most lists.
>  
> **What does moving back to the states mean? Does that mean closing the Education Department?** 
>  
> A virtual closure of Department of Education in Washington.
>  
> **Virtual closure?** 
>  
> Well, you're going to need some people just to make sure they're teaching English in the schools. Okay, you know English and mathematics, let's say. But we want to move education back to the states. If you look at the states, if you look at some of the individual countries, Norway is a very strong educational country, but many. I think Iowa, and I think Indiana, and a lot of these states that are well-run states. We have a lot of them that are very well run. When they run their own educational program, I think it's going to, I think they'll be able to compete with anybody. Then you're going to have the badly run states, like a guy like Gavin Newscum \[sic] in California, where he does a poor job, and he'll, but even in California, you'll give it to Riverside. You'll give it, you know, you'll give it to areas of California where I think they'll run a great school program.

The Department of Education was created as part of the 1979 [Department of Education Organization Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Education_Organization_Act). The closure of the Department of Education [would likely require an act of Congress](https://www.vox.com/education/384779/department-of-education-trump-musk-betsy-devos), as creation of federal offices is a power [authorized to Congress](https://www.law.cornell.edu/constitution-conan/article-2/section-2/clause-2/creation-of-federal-offices).

At times in the past, Congress has granted [presidential reorganization authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_reorganization_authority), delegating Congress' power over federal offices to the president for a limited period of time, and often subject to oversight such as Congressional nullification within a certain time period after president issued such an order. Reorganization authority was [most recently granted in 1984](https://www.heritage.org/political-process/report/the-presidents-reorganization-authority) to President Ronald Reagan, though Reagan did not use his reorganization authority. In 2012, President Barack Obama [requested reorganization authority](https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2012/01/13/government-reorganization-fact-sheet) stating his first act under the authority would be to consolidate six departments and agencies dealing with the business oversight into one.

This question will resolve as **Yes** if, before January 1, 2026, the United States has taken either of the following steps to eliminate the Department of Education:

* Passed a bill into law that would eliminate the Department of Education.
* Congress has granted [presidential reorganization authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_reorganization_authority) that gives the president power to reorganize the government, with **both** of the following subsequently occurring:
  * the president has issued an order under such power to eliminate the Department of Education
  * any oversight procedures specified in the reorganization authority passed by Congress have completed (for example, if a time limit is set on Congress to nullify such presidential orders, the time limit has expired without nullification)

The law need not take effect before the specified date, the passage of any law that abolishes the Department of Education at a future date is sufficient.

**Special education enforcement would be up to states under Trump plan**
Under the Trump administration’s plan to dismantle the U.S. Department of Education, federal oversight of special education enforcement would be transferred to states, raising concerns among educators, parents, and disability rights advocates. The administration fired nearly all staff in the Office for Civil Rights responsible for enforcing the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), though a federal judge blocked the layoffs following a lawsuit by federal worker unions. IDEA guarantees students with disabilities a free appropriate public education in the least restrictive environment, but federal funding covers only about 10.9% of the estimated 40% per-pupil cost promised under the law. In 2022–2023, approximately 7.5 million students—15% of public school enrollment—received special education services. Without federal oversight, critics fear states may lack the resources or political will to ensure compliance, as seen in past cases like Texas, where special education services were capped at 8.5% of students regardless of need, and Virginia, which failed to resolve parent complaints due to inadequate systems. Idaho faces a $82.2 million funding gap, and its state superintendent has made special education funding a top legislative priority. States like Iowa and Alabama have introduced legislation in response, with some lawmakers questioning federal oversight and others warning of eroded civil rights protections. Critics, including special education advocate Lisa Lightner, argue that the dismantling of federal infrastructure will cause long-term damage, noting that even 'normal' levels of service have historically failed many students. Federal intervention has been critical in protecting students’ rights, particularly during periods like Jim Crow, when state governments resisted integration. The Trump administration’s 'Returning Education to the States' tour emphasizes state autonomy, but experts warn that removing federal accountability could leave vulnerable students without essential services. According to Quinn Perry of the Idaho School Boards Association, 'We still have a federal mandate to provide services to these kids,' underscoring that the law remains unchanged, but enforcement may not be.

**Trump Vows to End U.S. Dependence on Chinese Rare Earths in 18 Months; Lawmakers Back Falun Gong Lawsuit Against Cisco**
U.S. President Donald Trump announced on November 2, 2025, during an interview on CBS's '60 Minutes' that the United States has launched an 'emergency action plan' to end reliance on Chinese rare earth minerals and critical minerals within 18 months. The plan, aimed at securing domestic and allied supply chains, includes new partnerships with Japan, Australia, and the United Kingdom. Trump stated, 'We have launched an emergency action plan, and within one or one and a half years, we will have everything we need, no matter what threats we face.' U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent echoed this, telling CNN that the rare earth crisis has prompted allies to act 'at an astonishing pace' to build alternative supply chains, with the Trump administration expected to eliminate Chinese threats within one to two years. Separately, two prominent U.S. Republican lawmakers—Representative Chris Smith, Chair of the U.S. Congressional-Executive Commission on China, and Representative John Moolenaar, Chair of the House Select Committee on China—sent a letter on October 29, 2025, urging the Trump administration to support the lawsuit filed by Falun Gong practitioners against Cisco Systems. The lawsuit, initiated in 2011, alleges that Cisco helped the Chinese government develop the 'Golden Shield Project,' enabling real-time identification and surveillance of Falun Gong practitioners, leading to arrests and torture. The lawmakers emphasized that 'a U.S. technology company designing tools for the persecution of a religious minority is a serious allegation' and urged the U.S. Supreme Court to allow the case to proceed. The Supreme Court is currently reviewing Cisco’s appeal to dismiss the case, and the U.S. Solicitor General, D. John Sauer, is expected to submit a written statement in early 2026.

**Trump '60 Minutes' interview: Here's what happened | FOX6 Milwaukee**

Regarding inflation, he claimed grocery prices are falling, despite September data showing a 0.3% monthly increase and a 2.7% year-over-year rise. On national security, Trump asserted the U.S. is the only country not testing nuclear weapons and said he would change that, citing Russia and China as nations that conduct underground tests. He downplayed the likelihood of war with Venezuela, though military strikes have killed at least 61 people in 14 attacks since early September without congressional authorization. On domestic policy, he affirmed his authority to invoke the Insurrection Act to deploy military forces in American cities, though he stated he has not chosen to do so. Trump praised the new ownership of CBS by Paramount under CEO David Ellison, calling it a positive development for the press, signaling improved relations with CBS News following past tensions. The interview was conducted amid a broader context of political and media dynamics, including the merger approval of Paramount and Skydance Media.

**Rep. Schrier addresses shutdown, other national issues in Wenatchee town hall - The Leavenworth Echo**
U.S. Representative Kim Schrier (D-Wash.) held a town hall meeting at Wenatchee Valley College on October 28, 2025, to address constituents on national issues including the ongoing government shutdown since October 1, 2025, due to Congress’s failure to pass 2026 fiscal year appropriations. Schrier criticized the shutdown as 'frustrating and unnecessary,' stating she had deferred her pay until the government reopened, and condemned Republican leaders and President Trump for excluding Democrats in negotiations. She emphasized that constituents elected her to advocate, not simply endorse pre-drafted plans. Schrier highlighted urgent healthcare concerns, noting that open enrollment for health insurance began on November 1 and tax credits were set to expire, expressing alarm over cuts to Medicaid, Planned Parenthood, and SNAP benefits. She stressed the need for affordable coverage to prevent a rise in the uninsured. Audience questions covered immigration, women’s rights, agricultural economic pressures, democracy, and public lands, to which Schrier responded with empathy and a commitment to continued advocacy. On U.S. military aid to Israel, Schrier acknowledged the moral complexity, stating the conflict began with Hamas’s attack on October 7, 2023, and calling it a defensive war. She affirmed her long-standing calls for the release of hostages and for injured children in Gaza to receive medical care in the U.S., expressing cautious hope for a lasting pause in hostilities. Schrier also denounced the Department of Energy’s cancellation of $1 billion in funding for the Pacific Northwest Hydrogen Hub, alleging it was retaliation for Washington being a 'blue state,' and warned the move undermined billions in private investment. She stated that both parties are opposing the administration on this issue. Closing the event, Schrier urged constituents to maintain community connections, avoid echo chambers, and bridge political divisions, declaring, 'Really united we stand, divided we fall.'

**Trump Says No SNAP: This Is All On Democrats, And We Won't Budge**
President Donald Trump stated on November 4, 2025, that Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits—commonly known as food stamps—would remain suspended for tens of millions of Americans until Senate Democrats reopen the government. Trump claimed the delay is due to Democrats’ refusal to pass a continuing resolution, asserting that SNAP benefits were excessively expanded under former President Joe Biden due to 'haphazard' distribution to anyone who asked, rather than only those in need. A federal judge had ordered the administration to use emergency funds to partially support SNAP, with a $4.65 billion payment made, but the process could take 'a few weeks to up to several months.' The government has been shut down since October 1, 2024, and Democrats have rejected 13 continuing resolution proposals, demanding healthcare subsidies in exchange. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) confirmed there are no funds for SNAP due to the shutdown. USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins accused Democrats of obstructing efforts to prevent fraud, claiming that 21 blue states refused to provide SNAP data and two even sued the USDA. Rollins asserted that in the 29 cooperating states, 'massive fraud' was already uncovered, alleging that Democrats are protecting illegal immigrants to preserve political power, warning that if benefits stop, 'those illegals will go back home' and Democrats would lose over 20 seats after the next census. Rollins added that 'a new sheriff is in town' under Trump, who will not tolerate 'waste, fraud, or abuse' while Americans go hungry. Currently, 42 million Americans receive SNAP benefits, with federal spending reaching nearly $100 billion in 2024 and an average monthly benefit of $187.20 per recipient.

**7 big questions hang over US politics heading into Election Day 2025**
The 2025 off-year elections on November 4 are shaping up as critical barometers of national political sentiment following Donald Trump's re-election in 2024. Key races include gubernatorial contests in New Jersey and Virginia, a high-stakes ballot measure in California (Proposition 50), state Supreme Court retention elections in Pennsylvania, and mayoral races in major cities like New York City. Proposition 50, backed by Governor Gavin Newsom, seeks to bypass California’s independent redistricting commission to draw more Democratic-leaning congressional districts in response to Trump’s push for GOP-friendly redistricting in red states. This move could counterbalance Republican gains in other states and influence control of the U.S. House. The results will be closely watched as a precursor to the 2026 midterms, when control of Congress will be decided. Seven major questions are emerging: Which party has momentum? Can California’s redistricting effort check Trump’s agenda? Will Proposition 50 boost Newsom’s 2028 presidential ambitions? Does anti-Trump messaging still resonate with swing voters? Are Trump’s policies backfiring, especially in states like Virginia and New Jersey affected by government shutdowns and federal funding cuts? How will Democratic internal divisions—between moderates and progressives—play out in races like New York City’s mayoral contest, where socialist candidate Zohran Mamdani leads? And which other races, such as mayoral elections in Detroit, Minneapolis, and Pittsburgh, or Pennsylvania’s Supreme Court retention vote, could have national implications, particularly on issues like federal troop deployment and election litigation? The outcomes will inform both party strategies heading into the 2026 midterms and the 2028 presidential primary.

**Judge orders Trump administration to restore school mental health grants**
A federal judge, Kymberly K. Evanson of the Western District of Washington, ordered the Trump administration to restore over $1 billion in congressionally approved grants for school-based mental health services, reversing cuts made in April 2025. The grants, established in response to the 2022 Uvalde school shooting that killed 19 students and two teachers, were intended to expand access to counseling and reduce financial barriers to becoming school psychologists. The Education Department had halted funding, citing President Donald Trump’s January 2025 executive order opposing diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives, and replaced the grants with a new competition emphasizing 'non-ideological' criteria. However, Judge Evanson ruled the cuts unconstitutional, stating Congress had repeatedly reaffirmed the need for school mental health services and that the funding cuts caused layoffs, reduced graduate student retention, and removed critical resources from rural and underserved communities. The decision affects 16 states—California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Mexico, Nevada, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Washington, and Wisconsin—that sued the Department, arguing the cuts disrupted services for nearly 775,000 students. In New York, $7.6 million in funds will be restored. The National Association of School Psychologists called the grants essential in addressing nationwide shortages of mental health professionals. The Education Department defended the cuts, claiming some recipients used funds for race-based recruitment, but Judge Evanson ordered the government to submit a compliance report within 48 hours. The agency has vowed to appeal the injunction.

**Education layoffs likely mean more students slipping through cracks**
The U.S. Department of Education is undergoing significant staff reductions, with 466 employees laid off on Friday as part of a planned reduction of over 4,200 positions, representing nearly 20% of its workforce. This marks the second major round of cuts during President Donald Trump's tenure, resulting in the department losing more than half of its staff. The reductions, linked to the ongoing federal shutdown and political pressure on Democratic legislators, threaten critical functions including special education services, civil rights enforcement, after-school programming, and the administration of federal funding such as Title I and Pell Grants. States dependent on federal education funding will be particularly affected. The Department of Education does not operate local schools but coordinates federal policy, enforces civil rights, and ensures compliance with federal mandates. Its discretionary budget is approximately $80 billion annually, supplemented by large mandatory spending for student aid. Despite the federal role being supplemental—supplying about 10% of K-12 funding—its oversight is pivotal in protecting underserved students and maintaining national standards. The Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 proposes abolishing or drastically shrinking the department, a plan echoed in the Trump administration’s 2018 'Delivering Government Solutions in the 21st Century' reorganization proposal. Experts warn that these cuts will exacerbate achievement gaps, delay funding distribution, and increase student and parent disputes, especially in special education. According to the National Education Association, the department has already begun withholding school funding for fiscal year 2025, and the Government Accountability Office has highlighted systemic risks from the staffing crisis. The article notes that at-risk students will be disproportionately impacted, as federally coordinated programs face administrative slowdowns and reduced capacity.

**Trump campaigned on closing the Education Department. Reality is more difficult.**
U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order on March 20 2025 to shrink the Department of Education, a move that would require congressional approval to fully dissolve the agency. Trump’s plan includes mass layoffs and the transfer of certain services to other agencies, and a Supreme Court ruling in July temporarily cleared the way for the administration to proceed with these cuts.  However, GOP‑controlled Congress has stalled the agency’s abolition.  In the Senate, Republicans hold 53 seats, short of the 60‑vote threshold needed to advance most legislation, and the House Committee on Education and Workforce has not yet voted on any of the four bills introduced by Representatives Thomas Massie, David Rouzer, Barry Moore and Nathaniel Moran.  Senate leaders, including Sen. Mike Rounds, Sen. Jim Banks and Sen. Tim Sheehy, reintroduced a companion bill in April, while Sen. Rand Paul reintroduced a similar measure in March with Sen. Mike Lee and Sen. Bernie Moreno.  Appropriations have also posed a hurdle: the Senate Appropriations Committee advanced a bipartisan bill in July that allocates $79 billion in discretionary funding for fiscal 2026—roughly the current level—and rejects Trump’s $12 billion cut proposal.  The House Appropriations subcommittee, however, advanced a spending proposal on September 2 that calls for $67 billion, aligns more closely with Trump’s cut priorities, and cuts Title I grant funding by $5.2 billion, while both chambers keep the Pell Grant maximum at $7,395.  The Department of Education’s 45‑year history and the need for congressional approval make its closure a complex, ongoing political battle.  "Our intentions are to ultimately dissolve the Department of Education — we know we have to do that in a way that makes sense and so, we’ll take a look at all bills," said House Committee Chair Tim Walberg.  "I can’t say whether they will all come up or not, but we know that, working with the secretary of Education, we’re going to right‑size it, and some things we’ll eliminate, other things we’ll shift, as we’ve done already, over to the Department of Labor to take on some workforce areas," Walberg added.

**Donald Trump Wants to Eliminate that Department of Education; Can He Do It?**
During the 2016 U.S. presidential election, Donald Trump, now President-elect, pledged to eliminate the U.S. Department of Education, stating in his book 'Great Again: How to Fix Our Crippled America' that 'a lot of people believe the Department of Education should just be eliminated. Get rid of it. If we don’t eliminate it completely, we certainly need to cut its power and reach.' Trump argued that the rising cost of college and the burden of student debt reflect systemic failures, which he attributes to federal overreach in education. According to Harvard legal scholar Laurence Tribe, while there is no constitutional barrier preventing Congress from abolishing the Department of Education, such an action would require a new act of Congress—meaning Trump cannot unilaterally eliminate it. However, Trump’s 100-day plan indicates an intention to shift educational oversight to local communities, suggesting a significant reorganization of federal education authority rather than outright abolition. The article notes that Trump’s claim, though initially seen as extreme, has gained credibility due to his impending presidency.

summary: All expert forecasts agree that the probability of the US eliminating the Department of Education through law or presidential reorganization before 2026 is extremely low—typically in the 1-5% range. Experts across public administration, political science, legal studies, and federal policy advocacy stress several converging themes: (1) The base rate for abolishing a cabinet-level department is virtually zero, with no precedent since World War II.
